title: CPU scheduling
relevance: Campus OAs and SDE interviews ask candidates to simulate schedulers on Gantt charts and compute turnaround/waiting/response times from arrival and burst data.
company_notes: Cisco-style online assessments reuse templates that ask for average turnaround time under preemptive SJF and under preemptive priority.

phases.goal: Establish what the CPU scheduler chooses among ready processes, preemptive vs non-preemptive mode, and the four derived timing metrics.

must_hit.point: The CPU scheduler picks one process from the ready queue using a criterion (arrival time, burst length, priority, or time quantum) and a mode (non-preemptive or preemptive).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names ready queue, a criterion, and that mode is whether a running process can be interrupted.

must_hit.point: Non-preemptive means a process keeps the CPU until its burst finishes or it blocks; preemptive means it can be interrupted and returned to the ready queue when another process becomes more deserving.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts run-to-completion vs interrupt-and-requeue under the algorithm's criterion.

must_hit.point: Arrival Time is when a process enters the ready queue; Burst Time is the CPU time it requires.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Defines AT and BT without mixing them with derived metrics.

must_hit.point: Completion Time is when the process finishes; TAT = CT − AT; WT = TAT − BT; RT is time from arrival until first CPU allocation.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States all four definitions and the TAT/WT/RT relationships as given.

must_hit.point: In non-preemptive scheduling RT equals WT because the first CPU allocation starts the only unbroken run; they diverge only under preemption.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explains why RT=WT without preemption and that preemption splits first start from total waiting.

probes: What does the CPU scheduler decide, and how do turnaround, waiting, and response time differ?

hints.1: Start from the ready queue and what the algorithm keys on.
hints.2: Define AT and BT, then CT, TAT, WT, and RT from those.
hints.3: State TAT=CT−AT, WT=TAT−BT, RT=first CPU time−AT, and that RT=WT only when non-preemptive.

phases.goal: Show how FCFS, SJF, SRTF, Round Robin, priority, multilevel queue, and multilevel feedback queue actually dispatch work.

must_hit.point: FCFS runs processes in arrival order, non-preemptively; the CPU can sit idle until the next arrival even if later work exists (as in idle from 4 to 5 before P3).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes arrival-order non-preemptive dispatch and idle gap between finished work and next arrival.

must_hit.point: Non-preemptive SJF, among already-arrived processes, picks smallest burst time and runs it to completion; equal bursts break by arrival order (then process number).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions arrived-set selection by BT, no mid-run preemption, and tie-break by arrival.

must_hit.point: SRTF always runs the process with smallest remaining burst; a shorter remaining arrival preempts the current process.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says remaining time, not original BT, and preemption on a shorter newcomer.

must_hit.point: Round Robin gives each ready process at most one time quantum, then preempts unfinished work to the back of the ready queue; arrivals during a quantum enqueue before the preempted process is re-added.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States TQ cap, back-of-queue reinsert, and during-quantum arrivals ahead of the preempted job.

must_hit.point: Preemptive priority always runs the highest-priority ready process; a higher-priority arrival immediately displaces the running one; aging raises priority of long waiters to fight starvation.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Highest priority wins, new higher priority preempts, aging as starvation remedy.

must_hit.point: With CPU→I/O→CPU bursts, a process leaves the CPU for I/O and is not contending; return times and priority reshape the schedule and can create idle CPU gaps while jobs are still in the system.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explains leave/return for I/O, others run meanwhile, idle gaps possible despite jobs present.

must_hit.point: MLQ uses fixed-priority queues by process type with no migration between queues; MLFQ demotes a process that exhausts its quantum to the next queue (often with larger quantum), with the last queue FCFS.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts permanent queue assignment vs demotion on unfinished quantum, last level FCFS.

probes: Walk through how SRTF and Round Robin decide who runs next at each event, and how MLQ differs from MLFQ.

hints.1: Pick one algorithm and say its criterion and mode first.
hints.2: For SRTF re-check remaining time at every arrival; for RR track the ready-queue order around quantum expiry.
hints.3: SRTF: shortest remaining preempts; RR: TQ then back of queue with mid-quantum arrivals ahead; MLQ no move, MLFQ demote on unfinished quantum.

phases.goal: Surface what each policy optimizes and what it costs (waiting, response, fairness, starvation, context switches).

must_hit.point: Non-preemptive SJF minimizes average waiting time for a fixed set of jobs available together, but cannot react to a short job arriving while a long job is already running.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States the fixed-set WT optimality claim and the mid-run short-job blind spot.

must_hit.point: RR keeps response time small—no process waits longer than (n−1)×TQ for its first slice—but pays with more context switches (each Gantt boundary between different processes is a switch).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Gives the first-slice bound in terms of n and TQ and links Gantt process changes to context switches.

must_hit.point: Priority scheduling can starve low-priority processes under a continuous stream of high-priority arrivals; aging is the standard remedy.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names starvation of low priority and aging as the fix.

must_hit.point: MLFQ approximates shortest-job-first without knowing burst times: short jobs finish in early small-quantum queues; long jobs sink to FCFS; doubling quanta (2, 4, 8) limit how often a long job is preempted.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Connects demotion/small early TQ to SJF-like behavior and doubling quanta to fewer preemptions for long jobs.

probes: When would you prefer SJF, SRTF, RR, or MLFQ, and what do you give up in each case?

hints.1: Compare what each optimizes: waiting time, response time, or fairness under unknown bursts.
hints.2: Contrast non-preemptive SJF's fixed-set WT property with RR's response bound and priority starvation.
hints.3: SJF: best average WT for a fixed arrived set but blind mid-run; RR: first slice within (n−1)×TQ with more switches; priority needs aging; MLFQ demotes long jobs without knowing BT.

phases.goal: Simulate schedules correctly under event-driven re-evaluation, including OA-style average TAT and priority-convention checks.

must_hit.point: For preemptive SJF/priority OA drills, build the Gantt by deciding at every arrival and every completion, then average TAT = CT − AT.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says event-driven re-evaluation at arrivals and completions, then average of CT−AT.

must_hit.point: In the five-process preemptive SJF template, forgetting to preempt when a shorter job arrives mid-run (for example P2→P3 at t=3) is the most common error; re-evaluate the ready set at every arrival.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Calls out mid-run shorter arrival preemption and re-check on every arrival, with the t=3 P2→P3 case.

must_hit.point: Priority convention must be confirmed before scheduling: some examples use higher number = higher priority, others lower number = higher priority; flipping the convention flips the Gantt.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States both conventions appear and that misreading the direction invalidates the chart.

must_hit.point: Under preemption, response time is not the same as waiting time (for example RR P1 has RT=0 and WT=7 because it is repeatedly preempted).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Gives a concrete RT vs WT split under preemption rather than equating them.

probes: Given arrival times, bursts, and either remaining-time or priority rules, produce the Gantt chart and average turnaround time.
Which priority convention is this problem using, and where would a missed preemption change CT?

hints.1: List events: each arrival and each completion.
hints.2: At every event pick shortest remaining or highest priority per the stated convention, then compute each TAT=CT−AT and average.
hints.3: Re-evaluate on every arrival (not only completions); confirm whether smaller or larger priority number wins before drawing the Gantt.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: Non-preemptive SJF gives minimum average waiting time for a fixed set of jobs available together but cannot yield to a short job that arrives mid-burst; SRTF preempts on smaller remaining time so it can react, at the cost of preemption and possible starvation of a long job that arrived first.

tradeoffs.topic: Round Robin response time vs context switches
tradeoffs.strong_answer: RR bounds time to first slice by (n−1)×TQ and improves response fairness, but every boundary between different processes on the Gantt is a context switch, so smaller quanta raise switch overhead.
Always running the highest-priority ready process can starve low-priority work under continuous high-priority arrivals; aging gradually raises a waiting process's priority so it eventually runs.

tradeoffs.topic: Multilevel Queue vs Multilevel Feedback Queue
tradeoffs.strong_answer: MLQ permanently assigns a process to a type-specific queue with no migration; MLFQ demotes processes that exhaust their quantum so short jobs leave early queues quickly while long jobs fall to FCFS, approximating SJF without knowing burst lengths in advance.

Scheduling only CPU bursts misses that I/O removes a process from CPU contention and that I/O return times create idle gaps and reorder who is eligible; the schedule cannot be read from burst lengths alone.

gotchas.trap: Assuming FCFS never idles if future work exists.
gotchas.correction: FCFS can leave the CPU idle until the next arrival (for example idle from 4 to 5 before P3 arrives).

gotchas.trap: Equating response time with waiting time under every algorithm.
gotchas.correction: RT equals WT only in non-preemptive runs; under preemption a process can start early and wait again later (for example RR P1: RT=0, WT=7).

gotchas.trap: Convoy effect ignored when praising FCFS simplicity.
gotchas.correction: A long early burst forces many short jobs to wait, inflating average waiting time.

gotchas.trap: SJF tie between equal burst times left undefined.
gotchas.correction: Break ties by arrival order, then by process number (for example equal BT 4: earlier arrival runs first).

gotchas.trap: In Round Robin, re-adding the preempted process before processes that arrived during its quantum.
gotchas.correction: Arrivals during the quantum enqueue before the preempted process is placed back on the ready queue.

gotchas.trap: Forgetting SRTF preemption when a shorter job arrives mid-run.
gotchas.correction: Re-evaluate remaining times at every arrival, not only at completions (classic miss: P2→P3 at t=3 in the five-process template).

gotchas.trap: Assuming one universal meaning of priority numbers.
gotchas.correction: Some problems treat higher number as higher priority, others treat lower number as higher priority—confirm before building the Gantt.

gotchas.trap: Believing MLQ can promote a batch job into a system queue.
gotchas.correction: MLQ has no migration; a process stays in its assigned queue for life—MLFQ is what allows movement via demotion.

gotchas.trap: Reading an I/O-aware schedule as if all bursts were pure CPU contention.
gotchas.correction: While a process is in I/O it does not contend for the CPU; return times drive idle gaps and preemption, so completion order is not determined by CPU bursts alone.
